concepts.label: Gradients through deep networks are products of many per-layer factors (Jacobians); factors below 1 make the product decay exponentially toward zero (vanishing), factors above 1 make it grow exponentially toward infinity (exploding)
Initialization determines whether and how well training converges (master-ai frames it as control of activation/gradient magnitudes; the course frames it as the starting point on the loss landscape)

Zero (or any identical-constant) initialization fails by the symmetry problem: all neurons in a layer compute the same output, receive the same gradient, make identical updates, collapsing the layer to a single effective neuron
Too-large initial weights make activations and gradients grow exponentially with depth, overflowing to inf/NaN and diverging training
Too-small initial weights make activations and gradients shrink exponentially with depth; the network collapses toward a constant function and early layers stay frozen
Random initialization must be variance-calibrated to the architecture: uncalibrated Gaussians N(0,0.01) and N(0,1) fail because activation variance drifts from layer to layer
Xavier's defining conditions: keep activation variance constant forward (Var(w) = 1/n_in) and gradient variance constant backward (Var(w) = 1/n_out)
Because n_in and n_out differ, Glorot & Bengio (2010) combined the forward and backward conditions into the Xavier variance 2/(n_in + n_out)
Xavier sampling formulas: normal N(0, sqrt(2/(n_in+n_out))) and uniform U(-sqrt(6/(n_in+n_out)), sqrt(6/(n_in+n_out)))
Xavier initialization is designed for symmetric, saturating activations (tanh, sigmoid) that are approximately linear near zero
He/Kaiming (2015): ReLU zeros out about half its inputs, halving the variance, so the init variance must be doubled to 2/n_in
Kaiming sampling formulas (N(0, sqrt(2/n_in)) and U(-sqrt(6/n_in), sqrt(6/n_in))) and the fan_in vs fan_out modes mapping to forward- vs backward-pass variance preservation
Init must match the activation: Xavier/Glorot for tanh/sigmoid, He/Kaiming for ReLU; Xavier-on-ReLU is about 2x too small (slow, suboptimal) and Kaiming-on-sigmoid saturates
The sigmoid derivative is capped at 0.25 (at x=0) and saturates toward zero away from the origin, so gradients shrink by at least 4x per sigmoid layer
tanh is better than sigmoid (maximum derivative 1.0 at x=0, four times sigmoid's 0.25) but still saturates for large |x|, so gradients still vanish through many layers, just more slowly
Consequence of vanishing gradients: early layers learn extremely slowly or not at all, so the learned feature hierarchy breaks (early feature extractors stay at random initialization)
Exploding gradients: causes (poor init, too-high learning rate with positive feedback) and symptom signature (NaN loss/weights, violent oscillations, huge weights), with sudden catastrophic onset
Loss-curve spikes are instability warnings that must be investigated (often gradient explosions / too-high init variance), not dismissed as training noise

RNNs are especially vulnerable: the same recurrent weight matrix is applied at every timestep, so the gradient product raises one matrix to a high power and its growth factor (spectral radius / largest singular value) decides everything

ReLU as the activation-side fix: derivative exactly 1 for active neurons (0 otherwise), no saturation on the positive side, so the gradient passes through unattenuated and very deep networks become trainable
The dying ReLU problem (permanently inactive neurons with zero gradient) and the Leaky ReLU / PReLU fixes (small non-zero negative-side gradient; learned slope from the same He et al. 2015 paper)
Normalization (BatchNorm/LayerNorm) as a stability solution: normalizing activations keeps them at a stable scale, preventing multiplicative blow-up/shrinkage and activation saturation

Residual connections fix vanishing gradients: y = x + F(x) has Jacobian I + dF/dx, so the identity term guarantees gradient flow (at least the next layer's gradient) and makes 100+ layer networks trainable

Gradient clipping mechanism: cap the gradient norm at threshold c by rescaling (direction preserved), bounding the update at lr*c; norm clipping is standard (c = 1.0) and preferred over value clipping which can distort direction
Clipping is symptomatic treatment, not a root-cause fix: it cannot help vanishing gradients and must not become a crutch masking bad init/LR/architecture (frequent clipping is a red flag)

Primary diagnostic practice: log gradient norms per layer (healthy training has roughly constant norms across layers; steady decline means vanishing, spikes mean instability) and monitor from the very first steps

Worked numerical demonstrations of sigmoid-network gradient decay (master-ai's 20-layer MNIST norm table vs the course's 0.25-decay diagram and alpha^(L-l) compounding table) - distinct artifacts illustrating the same exponential decay

Solution families for vanishing/exploding gradients and their deliberate combination in modern architectures (master-ai enumerates seven families incl. gates/attention/init; the course enumerates four; both say they are used together and enable very deep networks)
Fine-tuning rule: the initialization IS the pretrained weights - do not re-init them; only newly added layers need explicit initialization, and that init matters much less
Verify initialization empirically: forward a random input through the freshly initialized network and check that activation magnitudes/variances stay roughly constant across layers
Seed and scheme fixing for reproducibility: run-to-run variance traces to unfixed seeds/initialization; reproduce results with the same init scheme and random seed

PyTorch manual-initialization workflow: torch.nn.init functions applied in place (xavier_normal_, kaiming_normal_ with fan_in/relu, kaiming_uniform_), biases zeroed, and a recursive init function applied via model.apply()
Rely on / know the PyTorch default initializations: master-ai endorses the framework defaults as well-chosen; the course documents them (Conv2d and Linear use Kaiming Uniform, fan_in, a = sqrt(5))

Historical placement: before 2010, ad-hoc/uncalibrated initialization kept deep networks untrainable; principled initialization (Glorot & Bengio 2010, He et al. 2015) was a prerequisite for the deep-learning revolution
Diagnostic priority when loss goes NaN: suspect exploding gradients / too-large weights first (check init, add clipping, reduce LR) before blaming the data pipeline or loss function
Bias initialization standard: zeros is the simple, standard default for bias parameters (with documented exceptions on the master-ai side)
